forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.85 is 10% below the Street consensus of $3.17, reflecting a more cautious view on the pace of steel pricing recovery and margin expansion. While I'm constructive on STLD's fundamental positioning - they benefit from IRA tailwinds, have a diversified business model, and excellent operational execution - I believe consensus is overly optimistic about how quickly metal spreads will normalize from Q4's compressed levels. Q4 2025 showed significant margin compression with gross margin falling to 11.8% from 15.7% in Q3, and while I expect improvement in Q1, I model 14.4% gross margin versus what appears to be ~15.5%+ implied by consensus.

The key data points driving my variant view: (1) HRC pricing has recovered but remains volatile - CRU data shows spot around $750/ton versus $700 in Q4, not the $800+ needed for meaningful margin expansion; (2) The massive Q4 inventory build ($540M increase) suggests either demand pull-forward or inventory accumulation that may need to work through the system; (3) Interest expense jumped to $27M in Q4 (from $13.6M in Q3) reflecting higher debt levels that will persist. On the positive side, the 6% dividend increase announced signals management confidence in cash generation, and the IRA-driven investment in green steel provides structural competitive advantages.

What would change my mind: If HRC spot prices sustainably break above $800/ton in February-March, I would revise estimates higher by $0.15-0.20 EPS. Additionally, if Q1 shipment data shows stronger-than-typical seasonal patterns (>5% QoQ growth), that would indicate demand is healthier than I'm modeling. Conversely, if tariff policy creates import uncertainty leading to inventory destocking, there's downside risk to $2.50 EPS.

Operationally, I’m not calling a demand re-rate: consolidated revenue remains anchored near the recent seasonal run-rate (~$2.2B), with Beer stability offsetting continued Wine & Spirits softness. A sharper-than-expected Beer slowdown (depletions/promo) would also pressure both revenue and gross margin, pulling EPS toward (or below) consensus.

My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of ¥38.50 represents a 6.9% premium to Street consensus of ¥36.03, driven primarily by the market's underappreciation of share count reduction from Seven & i's aggressive buyback program. The share count trajectory shows a clear pattern: from 2.60B in Q4 FY25 to 2.44B in Q3 FY26 - a 6% reduction in three quarters. Assuming continued buyback pace of ~¥89B quarterly (conservative vs Q3's exceptional ¥162B), I project share count declining to approximately 2.18B. This mechanical EPS accretion of roughly 12% from share reduction alone drives my above-consensus call, even as I apply conservative operating assumptions.

The key uncertainty in my model is gross margin trajectory. Q3's 29.1% gross margin was anomalously high versus the ~19-21% range seen in Q1-Q2 and Q4 FY25. I'm assuming normalization to 26% in Q4 - still elevated but more sustainable than Q3's peak. If Q3's improvement was structural (perhaps from superstore divestitures improving mix), my estimates could prove conservative. Conversely, if gross margin reverts fully to historical ~20% levels, my EPS estimate would be at risk. The Walmart and CVS Q4 results provide supportive read-through for 7-Eleven North America operations, with both confirming healthy consumer spending patterns and steady retail execution.

I maintain medium-high conviction in this call because the share buyback math is mechanical and verifiable - we know the company has been aggressively repurchasing shares. The primary risk to my thesis is if management pivots capital allocation strategy due to Couche-Tard negotiations or other M&A optionality needs. I would revisit my estimates downward if Q4 buyback activity comes in below ¥60B or if gross margin shows signs of reverting below 24%.

The market consensus of ~$36 EPS (J-GAAP basis implied) structurally underestimates the 'pure-play' profitability resulting from the accelerated divestiture of the Ito-Yokado superstore assets. Wall Street models are dragging their feet on this margin reset, likely waiting for full-year confirmation.

Furthermore, my forecast anticipates strong operating leverage in Q4. Seasonally, Q4 is a high-volume quarter, and applying a 29% margin to Q4 volumes—even with conservative revenue estimates of $2,485B—generates significantly more Gross Profit dollars than consensus implies. While Q3 SG&A was elevated, I model only a modest efficiency gain (580B vs 590B in Q3), which is sufficient to drive Operating Income to ~145B, well ahead of the implied consensus run-rate.

Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging that if Q3's SG&A spike was due to sticky structural costs rather than one-time transaction fees, my EPS beat will narrow. However, even with Q3-level costs, the margin expansion alone supports a beat. The risk-reward asymmetry overwhelmingly favors a beat.

My Q4 2026 EPS forecast of ¥38.5 for Seven & i Holdings maintains my previous view and represents a fundamental rejection of the Wall Street consensus figure of $0.19, which is clearly erroneous due to a currency or data provider error. The historical EPS data demonstrates quarterly earnings consistently in the ¥19-42 range (Q4 2025: ¥42.14, Q3 2026: ¥33.0, Q2 2026: ¥29.0, Q1 2026: ¥19.0), making a $0.19 consensus mathematically impossible for a company generating ¥70-110B in quarterly net income. My estimate of ¥38.5 reflects a sequential improvement from Q3's ¥33.0 driven by typical Q4 seasonality benefits, while remaining below Q4 2025's exceptional ¥42.14 given year-over-year margin normalization.

The key drivers supporting my forecast are: (1) stable Japan convenience store performance with 2-3% SSS growth, validated by Walmart's Q4 results showing healthy consumer spending across income cohorts; (2) continued aggressive share buyback program that has reduced weighted average shares from 2.60B in Q4 2025 to an expected 2.35B in Q4 2026, providing meaningful EPS accretion; and (3) gross margin sustained near the 29% level achieved in Q3 2026, representing significant improvement from the sub-20% margins seen in Q1-Q2. The company's balance sheet deleveraging and capital allocation discipline continue to support earnings quality.

What would change my view: If Japanese consumer spending deteriorates materially (currently showing no signs of weakness), if the Couche-Tard acquisition drama escalates to disrupt operations, or if gross margins revert toward the depressed Q1-Q2 levels (~17-19%) rather than sustaining near Q3's 29%. The primary risk to my forecast is execution uncertainty around the supermarket restructuring program and any one-time charges that management might recognize in Q4 as a fiscal year-end quarter cleanup.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.53 is marginally below consensus of $0.55, reflecting a more conservative view on seasonal dynamics and competitive pressures. While AT&T demonstrated strong operational execution in Q4 2025 with an EPS beat of +10.6% ($0.52 vs $0.47 expected), this outperformance was partly driven by Q4-specific factors including holiday equipment strength and an anomalously low tax rate of 2.6%. Q1 typically sees a meaningful sequential revenue decline of 8-10% as equipment sales normalize, and I'm factoring in a return to normalized tax rates of 21-22% which creates a ~$0.02 headwind versus Q4.

The Street appears to be extrapolating Q4's momentum without fully accounting for seasonal patterns. Looking at Q1 2025, AT&T reported EPS of $0.51, and while the company has made operational improvements (particularly in fiber where net adds are running at ~260K/quarter), the Bernstein competitive warnings suggest 2026 will see intensified promotional activity from T-Mobile and Verizon. This competitive backdrop could pressure postpaid ARPU and increase subscriber acquisition costs. Additionally, the dramatic cash position improvement from $3.3B to $20.3B over the past year reflects strong operational execution, but Q1 will see cash deployment toward debt reduction and buybacks, not earnings accretion.

What would change my view: If management's fiber penetration accelerates beyond 260K quarterly adds or if competitive intensity proves less severe than Bernstein's warnings suggest, there's upside to $0.55-0.56. Conversely, if T-Mobile's Un-carrier promotions drive elevated churn above 1.0%, downside to $0.50 is plausible. The key swing factor is whether the 5G Standalone-native IoT platform with Cisco (announced in recent news) can drive incremental enterprise revenue sooner than expected.

While top-line revenue drops sequentially from Q4 due to lower equipment volumes, this 'lost' revenue is low-to-negative margin. Consequently, the operating margin profile improves significantly in Q1 as high-margin Service revenue comprises a larger portion of the pie. Coupled with aggressive $400M+ annualized cost take-outs realized in late 2025, this creates an earnings setup that will decouple from the flattish revenue trend.

My forecast of $0.57 EPS is slightly above the Street's $0.55, driven by a 120bps expected improvement in OpEx efficiency ratio YoY. The market is underestimating the stickiness of recent price increases in the Mobility segment and the 'net-add' resilience in Fiber, which provides a high-margin floor. I also project lower SG&A expenses than consensus, validating management's cost transformation rhetoric.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.01 remains significantly below Wall Street's $0.02 consensus (50% below), driven by a fundamental disagreement about Tanzania's mining tax regime. The Street's consensus mathematically requires an effective tax rate of approximately 30-35%, which contradicts the empirical evidence from Q1 2026 where TRX reported a 111% effective tax rate ($7.0M tax expense on $6.3M pre-tax income). While some of Q1's tax burden was likely timing-related (deferred tax liability increased $5.1M QoQ), the structural reality of Tanzanian mining royalties (6% of gross revenue), 30% corporate tax, and withholding taxes means a sustainable effective rate is likely 65-75%, not the 25-30% implied by consensus.

The February 19 roadshow with CEO Mullowney and CFO Leonard occurred but has produced no public clarity on the tax regime situation. The Roth Capital price target increase to $2.25 is sentiment-driven, not fundamentally justified - their note provides no granular tax analysis. The stock's 11% rally on February 10 reflects analyst momentum rather than resolution of the core uncertainty. Until management provides explicit guidance on normalized tax rates or we see actual Q2 results demonstrating tax normalization, I cannot justify moving toward consensus.

Operationally, TRX is executing well: Buckreef production is ramping as expected, gross margins remain excellent at 56%, and gold prices remain supportive above $2,050/oz. Revenue should grow to approximately $38M (+8.6% QoQ). However, the operational excellence is being overshadowed by tax uncertainty. My conviction remains low because the effective tax rate is genuinely unpredictable - I could be too conservative if Q1's rate was truly anomalous, but I refuse to assume away a demonstrated $7M quarterly tax expense without evidence.

UCB's NIM expanded 8 bps in Q3 2025 and the favorable repricing dynamics remain intact as their loan book continues to reprice at higher yields while deposit costs have stabilized. The new $100M buyback authorization signals management confidence in both earnings trajectory and capital position. Credit quality remains exceptionally strong - the Hurricane Helene reserve release in Q3 confirms their conservative provisioning approach. The Southeast regional banking market continues to provide solid loan demand and reasonable pricing.

Key risks to my above-consensus view include: (1) more aggressive deposit competition in their Southeast markets that could compress NIM faster than expected, (2) potential CRE credit deterioration that has affected other regional banks, and (3) seasonal Q1 weakness in fee income that could offset some NIM benefit. If deposit betas tick up materially or credit quality shows any signs of stress, I would revise my estimate downward. However, based on the historical pattern of execution and favorable rate dynamics, I maintain conviction in my above-consensus estimate.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.58 remains 15.3% above the Street consensus of $1.37, reflecting continued conviction that analysts systematically underestimate Unity Bancorp's earnings power. The bank has delivered four consecutive significant earnings beats: Q1 2025 (flat), Q2 2025 (+36.4%), Q3 2025 (+9.3%), and Q4 2025 (+11.8%). This persistent pattern of upside surprises indicates structural underestimation in Street models that fail to capture Unity's superior net interest margin franchise operating at 4.5% - approximately 130bps above the regional bank peer average.

The key drivers supporting my above-consensus estimate include: (1) Piper Sandler's January endorsement as a Top Bank Investment Idea for 2026, explicitly citing the durability of Unity's NIM and double-digit loan growth trajectory; (2) management's track record of conservative guidance that consistently results in beats; and (3) operating leverage from a lean cost structure with SG&A controlled at ~$12-13M quarterly. I would revisit my estimate upward if management provides clearer guidance on Frontier cost synergies or if wireless net adds show unexpected strength.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2025 forecast of -$0.14 EPS on $132M revenue remains unchanged from my prior estimate, reflecting the profound uncertainty created by the extended 3+ week earnings delay with zero company communication. The continued silence from management is now the dominant signal - well-functioning companies do not miss filing deadlines by this margin without explanation unless facing material audit complications, potential restatements, or going concern issues. The lack of any 8-K filing, press release, or investor update suggests this is not a minor administrative delay but rather a substantive issue requiring extended auditor work.

From a fundamental standpoint, Q4 2025 should show continued sequential improvement from the Q2 2025 disaster (when gross margins collapsed to 52.8% and the company took a $152M impairment charge). I model gross margins recovering to 65% as the one-time cost accounting issues normalize, with revenue roughly flat at $132M as Milk Makeup's prestige beauty momentum (+5% assumed) offsets continued Obagi professional channel weakness (-5%). However, SG&A remains elevated at ~82% of revenue due to ongoing legal/audit costs related to the securities investigation, resulting in an operating loss of -$23.7M.

The critical risk remains the balance sheet - I project ending cash of approximately $5M, down from $10.5M at Q2 2025, which represents an existential liquidity crisis requiring immediate capital action in Q1 2026. The extended earnings delay compounds this concern as it prevents the company from accessing capital markets and raises questions about whether auditors may issue a going concern qualification. If my forecast is materially wrong, it will likely be due to (1) additional impairment charges not yet disclosed, (2) worse-than-expected working capital consumption, or (3) surprise positive news such as an announced financing or strategic transaction that addresses the liquidity crisis.

My Q2 FY26 EPS estimate of $1.37 sits $0.02 (1.4%) below Street consensus of $1.39, maintaining my cautious stance on SG&A normalization timing. The central thesis remains unchanged: Q1 FY26 SG&A spiked to $63.5M—well above the historical $51-54M run rate—driven by distribution network transition costs that management explicitly stated won't yield benefits until FY27. While I expect modest sequential improvement to ~$62M in Q2 as some one-time transition costs moderate, the Street appears overly optimistic that cost discipline will return faster than management has guided.

The revenue picture is more constructive, with Q2 typically benefiting from seasonal Americas strength (DIY/maintenance demand) that historically drives 5-7% QoQ growth. I'm modeling $161M in revenue (+4.3% QoQ) which aligns with consensus. However, the margin story is where I diverge: I expect gross margin compression to ~55.3% from Q1's 56.2% as the inventory built in Q1 ($84M vs $79.9M in Q4) flows through COGS at slightly elevated costs. Combined with the stubborn SG&A structure, operating margin likely remains compressed at ~16.7% versus the 17-18% range the Street may be implicitly assuming.

What would change my view: Evidence that distribution optimization is tracking ahead of the FY27 timeline (no such signals in recent filings), or a meaningful reduction in G&A expenses below $60M that would suggest transition costs are normalizing faster. The board appointment of Ken Plunk (former J&J Snack Foods CFO) is a governance positive but has no near-term earnings implications. Insider buying patterns remain encouraging for long-term alignment but don't alter the Q2 cost structure reality.

forecasts.thesis:
My forecast diverges from the Wall Street consensus on the top line, projecting a revenue miss ($152.5M vs $160M) due to a rigorous application of seasonality patterns. The Street's estimate implies sequential revenue growth from Q1, a trend seen only once in the last decade for the Feb-ending quarter. WDFC's business is maintenance-driven, and Q2 represents the winter lull before spring/summer activity ramps up. I see the consensus as erroneously extrapolating Q4 strength or ignoring the normal ebb and flow of the maintenance cycle.

However, I project an EPS beat ($1.42 vs $1.39) driven by 'Quality over Quantity'. I expect Gross Margin to expand to 56.5% (vs 54.6% in the prior year period and ~56.2% in Q1), fueled by structural cost improvements and easing input prices. The recent appointment of Ken Plunk (ex-CFO) to the board reinforces a narrative of financial discipline, which should help rein in the anomalous SG&A spike seen in Q1. My model assumes OpEx normalizes toward ~$61M, protecting profitability despite the revenue softness.

I would be wrong if revenue accelerates sequentially, which would likely indicate a significant restocking cycle by major retailers (unexpected this early) or successful, rapid market share gains in premium products. Conversely, if the high Q1 SG&A represents a new structural baseline rather than timing-related expenses, my EPS thesis would break, pushing earnings closer to $1.20.

risks: SG&A stickiness: Q1 G&A was unusually high ($55.3M), risk of run-rate persistence

My Q1 2026 WFC EPS estimate of $1.58 sits modestly above the $1.56 consensus, driven by conviction in three key factors that the Street appears to be underweighting. First, the $150B 'YOLO' tax refund liquidity injection through March 2026 should provide a meaningful tailwind to wealth management inflows and fee income that consensus models may not fully capture. Second, the aggressive buyback program continues at ~$5.5B/quarter pace, mechanically reducing diluted shares from 3.22B to approximately 3.16-3.19B - this alone adds ~$0.02 to EPS versus static share count assumptions. The earnings call highlighted 'significant momentum' and 17% diluted EPS growth in 2025, signaling execution confidence. I expect Q1 operating expenses to rise ~$400M from seasonal resets (benefits, FICA), pushing efficiency ratio to ~62% from Q4's 57%.

My variant view versus consensus centers on the interplay between buyback-driven EPS accretion and fee income resilience. The Street may be too focused on NII headwinds while underestimating the mechanical benefit of aggressive capital return and the specific Q1 catalyst from tax refund wealth inflows. Key risks to my thesis include faster-than-expected deposit competition eroding NIM, or unexpected credit deterioration in commercial real estate. I would revisit my estimate if March economic data shows consumer weakness accelerating or if deposit outflows intensify.

forecasts.thesis:
I maintain my ¥43.50 Q4 2026 EPS estimate, representing a 6.2% discount to the Street consensus of ¥46.39. My variant view centers on margin recovery skepticism: while Q4 should see meaningful seasonal improvement from Q3's depressed 7.3% operating margin, I project only 10.7% (vs. the implied 11.0%+ embedded in consensus). The inventory overhang remains substantial at ¥216.5B, constraining the company's pricing power and gross margin recovery pace. Additionally, China exposure (~30% of sales) continues to weigh on the Motion Control segment, with peer data from MELCO and MHI confirming stable but not accelerating automation demand.

The key data points supporting my below-consensus view include: (1) Q3 2026 gross margin of 34.1% was well below Q4 2025's 36.4%, and I expect only partial recovery to 36.2%; (2) inventory levels increased sequentially in Q3 despite soft demand, signaling potential destocking headwinds; (3) while MKS's Q4 call confirmed semi equipment stabilization (modestly positive for Robotics), auto sector weakness continues to limit upside. My ¥148.5T revenue estimate aligns roughly with seasonal patterns but assumes Motion Control China remains flat versus Q3.

What would change my view: If management provides guidance suggesting stronger-than-expected order recovery in Motion Control Japan/US, or if inventory levels show meaningful decline in Q4 preliminary data, I would consider revising upward. Conversely, further China weakness or extended inventory destocking would validate my conservative stance. The 62% confidence level reflects reasonable visibility into seasonal patterns but uncertainty around margin recovery pace and geographic demand mix.

Inventory destocking extending into FY2027
Yen appreciation eroding translation gains
Semi equipment recovery slower than MKS signals suggest

forecasts.thesis: My differentiated view is that YASKAWA will miss consensus EPS by ~12.7% ($40.50 vs. $46.39 consensus) due to persistent industrial slowdown headwinds partially offset by typical Q4 seasonal strength. While the Street appears to be expecting stabilization, primary data from Japanese peer Mitsubishi Electric (reported Feb 2) indicates ongoing deterioration in industrial segments, contradicting stabilization narratives. Historical Q4 seasonality is strong (Q4 2025 revenue was $143.99B vs Q3 2026 $134.79B, +7.0% q/q) but likely insufficient to overcome macro weakness. My forecast reflects ~7% q/q revenue growth to $144.22B (seasonal) but flat YoY, with margin pressure from elevated inventory and higher short-term debt driving interest expense. I've revised my previous estimate down from $41.50 to $40.50 after deeper analysis of SG&A inflation and debt costs. My alpha comes from: (1) ignoring the 'stabilization' narrative contradicted by peer data, (2) focusing on margin deterioration from cost pressures and debt, and (3) properly weighting historical seasonality against cyclical headwinds. I would change my mind if new data shows industrial orders accelerating sharply or if yen weakness provides an unexpected boost.

My forecast stays modestly above consensus on revenue ($0.905B vs $0.88B) but below on EPS (44.7 vs 46.39). The Street is implicitly underwriting either a cleaner Robotics rebound and/or stronger operating leverage than I’m willing to assume without company-specific order/backlog evidence; I model Robotics as stable rather than sharply improving, which caps mix-driven margin upside.

The quarter’s EPS is most sensitive to (1) gross margin mix and (2) non-operating/FX. I assume modest gross-margin improvement and limited OpEx leverage, while allowing for a small non-operating tailwind; that combination yields an EPS outcome modestly below consensus despite a small revenue beat. I would change my view if there were clear, Yaskawa-specific indicators of a Robotics order upturn (backlog/book-to-bill commentary) or evidence of materially higher operating leverage (structural SG&A reductions).
